# Implementing CRDTs for Collaborative Editing

This skill describes how to design, implement, test, and deploy a Conflict-Free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) suitable for real-time collaborative editing (plain text, rich text, or structured documents). It walks through choosing the right CRDT model, designing identifiers and metadata, implementing core operations (insert, delete, update, merge), handling offline / asynchronous replicas, optimizing performance (compaction, tombstone GC), and validating correctness (convergence, commutativity, idempotence). It provides concrete pseudocode patterns, message formats, tests, and practical tips for production systems.

When to use
- Building a collaborative text editor, rich-text editor, or collaborative structured document (JSON/trees) where multiple users may edit concurrently, possibly offline.
- You need automatic conflict resolution without a central server coordinating edits.
- You want strong eventual consistency: all replicas converge

Agenten des Secret Service reagieren sofort und eröffnen das Feuer. Er soll Lehrer sein und sich als Gast ins Hilton eingemietet haben.

A ist derzeit im Krankenhaus und soll am Montag dem Richter vorgeführt werden. Das nächste Dinner müssen wir sicherer machen. Gegen 10 Uhr löste sich der Saal auf. Die Gäste mussten ihn durch einen anderen Ausgang verlassen. Der Ausgang, durch den wir hineingekommen waren, ist jetzt ein Tatort.

window: Uncertainty exists all around us. We established this in our last episode, but how can we embrace it rather than fighting it? That's what we're going to talk about in today's episode. My name is Jonathan Cattrall. You're listening to Developer T. My goal on the show is to coach you through the hardest parts of your career to provide you with information, insights, inspiration, conversations,

With people in this industry, as well as other industries, all kinds of conversations that we've had on this show, all in hopes of helping you become the great developer that you want to be. I've said it on a few episodes now, and I'm going to continue saying it. If you don't want to become a better developer than you are today, then you probably have no business listening to this show.

My goal is for you to walk away from listening to this challenged and optimistic, charged up, ready to take an action step today that will make you a better developer. We can take a very simple step each and every day to become better at what we do. Sometimes those steps are extremely practical. Sometimes they mean setting up your environment in a new way.

But sometimes they're not super practical. Instead, they're much more academic or perhaps theoretical. Mindset shifts, ways of thinking, ways of changing your thought patterns, ways of changing the way you view the world around you. And that's kind of what we're talking about in today's episode. We're talking about uncertainty. In the last episode, we established this idea of the law of conservation of uncertainty. What does that mean?

Well, it basically means that for any given project, and really for anything that you do in your life, a level of uncertainty exists. There are so many variables that go into any given decision. And so if we act like that uncertainty doesn't exist, then really all we're doing is shifting it to a different place.

But in the last episode, we also established the fact that humans are loss-averse. This shouldn't come as a surprise. There's tons of research already out there on the subject. But because of our loss-aversion, we seek certainty. We want to be as safe as possible with our bets. This goes for our money, and it goes for everything else that we do.

Full certainty puts those decisions into a different category. The things that we can be fully certain about. As developers, these things are few and far between. It's not bad news. And that's what we're talking about today. How to embrace this uncertainty.

Very often we try to sell certainty. This is such a common business practice. We want to sell a given product with all the features that you want for a fixed price and within a fixed timeline. All of these things mitigating uncertainty.

and ultimately viewing uncertainty as the enemy. But perhaps there's another way to do this. Perhaps we can embrace uncertainty. And instead of selling certainty, we sell change. Change is progressive.

Change is adaptive. If we sell change as a valuable aspect of what we do, we get a chance to create a scenario where adapting to a new market is easy, where adapting to a new staffing situation becomes second nature.

window: Every day, thousands of people, mostly American, mostly white, and mostly retired, come to this town looking for relief from the turmoil in their mouths. Here, dental care costs up to 80% less than what it might cost in the US. Dental tourism to Los Algodones is so common that many call this place Molar City. Today, there are nearly 1,000 dentists in this 7,000-person town, and 98% of those in the patient's chair traveled here from outside Mexico. Lasha is going to take it from here.

Watch any one of these YouTube videos, and you'll see how a trip to Molar City is made easy for an American. For decades, this crossing didn't even require a passport. In one video, a retired couple arrives at Arizona's edge. They do a 360, displaying the massive lot where they've just parked. "We love Mexico," they say emphatically, talking to the camera. The camera then pans to show the rust-colored border wall in front of them. That corrugated monstrosity. They marvel. Then a US Border Patrol vehicle starts driving past the screen, on guard, it seems, for anyone trying to cross in the opposite direction. To this, the camera woman speaks again, as if she's talking directly to Border Patrol. "Get 'em, boys," she says. Then they begin their walk into Mexico. In Los Algodones, there are dense clusters of medical offices and a canopy of billboards above them. Vendors are set up on sidewalks where they sell handmade goods and kitschy souvenirs, like this one graphic tee that says, "Keep calm, you're on the fun side of Trump's wall." And then there are the street promoters, people who are stationed at almost every street corner. Each of them competing for superlatives: the best deal, the quickest appointment, the most popular clinic in town. In Molar City, a street promoter is the first person a tourist will encounter.
Good morning, buddy.

Pharmacy?

I got dental promotion.

window: Every day, thousands of people, mostly American, mostly white, and mostly retired, come to this town looking for relief from the turmoil in their mouths. Here, dental care costs up to 80% less than what it might cost in the US. Dental tourism to Los Algodones is so common that many call this place Molar City. Today, there are nearly 1,000 dentists in this 7,000-person town, and 98% of those in the patient's chair traveled here from outside Mexico. Lasha is going to take it from here.

Watch any one of these YouTube videos, and you'll see how a trip to Molar City is made easy for an American. For decades, this crossing didn't even require a passport. In one video, a retired couple arrives at Arizona's edge. They do a 360, displaying the massive lot where they've just parked. "We love Mexico," they say emphatically, talking to the camera. The camera then pans to show the rust-colored border wall in front of them. That corrugated monstrosity. They marvel. Then a US Border Patrol vehicle starts driving past the screen, on guard, it seems, for anyone trying to cross in the opposite direction. To this, the camera woman speaks again, as if she's talking directly to Border Patrol. "Get 'em, boys," she says. Then they begin their walk into Mexico. In Los Algodones, there are dense clusters of medical offices and a canopy of billboards above them. Vendors are set up on sidewalks where they sell handmade goods and kitschy souvenirs, like this one graphic tee that says, "Keep calm, you're on the fun side of Trump's wall." And then there are the street promoters, people who are stationed at almost every street corner. Each of them competing for superlatives: the best deal, the quickest appointment, the most popular clinic in town. In Molar City, a street promoter is the first person a tourist will encounter.
Good morning, buddy.
What is it? Dental?
Pharmacy?
Glasses?
I got dental promotion.

Some promoters try to lure people in with discounts. Others vie for attention in more creative ways. Like dressing up in a full-body tooth costume and waving a sign. Then there's Alberto, a street promoter who takes a different approach altogether. He tries to attract customers with humor.
I'm always trying to make stuff funny, you know, make them laugh like a comedian almost, make them relax just for that second.
Alberto is employed by a couple clinics in town. He's assigned to a specific street corner where he stands all day and tries to make his commissions.

We also maintain dashboards for long-term trend analysis and visual monitoring. An interesting side effect appeared when we migrated to Xcode 26. Startup times on simulators suddenly increased overnight. At first, we suspected a regression in our codebase. Later, we discovered that simulators in Xcode 26 had becomes lower overall.

The slowdown affected every stage of the startup flow, while real devices remained unchanged. Without historical performance tracking, identifying this would have been much harder. Why we intentionally slowed down the internet in C. It seemed like the problem was solved, performance tests were running every night, alerts were coming into Slack, and we could track trends in a dashboard. But at some point after another release, we again saw a regression in app launch time for users.

A natural question came up, why did the issue still reach production if we already had automated performance tests in place? This time, startup degradation only affected users with slow internet connections. The application relies heavily on request caching to reduce the time between launch and reaching the target screen. In one release, the cache mechanism broke silently, forcing the application to wait for fresh server responses before entering the UI.

On fast office Wi-Fi, the issue was almost invisible. For users with unstable or slow connections, startup time increased dramatically. After that incident, we redesigned the test execution flow. The new process works like this. 1. The first 10 runs execute under normal network conditions. 2. During these runs, the application fills local caches. 3. Then the network is artificially degraded, bandwidth limited to 400 kilobits per second.

Latency increased to 200 miz. 4. The same scenarios execute again with cached data already present on the device. To emulate poor network conditions, we use Network Link Conditioner. This tool throttles the entire device network stack instead of individual requests, which makes the environment much closer to real-world usage.

This approach gives us two important validations simultaneously. First, if a new unexpected network request appears in the critical path, startup time immediately increases. Second, we automatically verify cache correctness. If caching works properly, startup performance remains nearly identical even under slow network conditions. If the app suddenly waits for the backend again, the regression becomes obvious.

Recently, this setup caught a subtle but critical issue. One developer modified logic inside the caching layer. During code review, the mistake looked almost harmless. From the code itself, it was difficult to predict any major impact.

window: 마지막으로 이직을 준비하면서도 이력서와 링크드인 프로필을 그대로 두는 경우가 많은데요. 이 역시 큰 실수로 지목이 됩니다. SICK은 새로운 분야에 지원할 때는 기존의 경력보다 전이 가능한 기술을 전면에 내세우는 것이 중요하다고 조언합니다. 예를 들어 프로젝트 관리 능력이나 의사소통 능력, 문제해결 능력은 업종이 달라져도 충분히 경쟁력이 될 수 있기 때문입니다.
그렇다면 실제로 직장을 바꾸는 방법에는 어떤 것들이 있을까요? 첫 번째는 직무와 산업계를 모두 바꾸는 경우를 살펴볼 수 있습니다. 역시나 가장 큰 변화인 만큼 준비도 가장 많이 필요하지만 새로운 커리어를 시작할 수 있는 방법으로 손꼽힙니다. 두 번째는 같은 산업계에서 직무만 바꾸는 겁니다.
예를 들어 IT업계에서 개발자가 프로젝트 매니저가 되거나 또 병원에서 임상업무 대신 행정업무를 맡는 방식인데요. 기존 산업에 대한 이해가 있기 때문에 새로운 일을 배우는 부담이 상대적으로 적다는 장점이 있습니다.
이어서 세 번째, 같은 직무를 유지하면서 업계만 바꾸는 겁니다. 회계사가 제조업에서 의료분야로 옮기거나 마케팅 담당자가 금융회사에서 교육기관으로 이직하는 것처럼 기존의 경험을 살리면서 새로운 환경을 경험하는 방법입니다. 업무는 익숙하지만 새로운 환경과 문화를 경험할 수 있어서 가장 현실적인 이직 방법 가운데 하나로 손꼽힙니다.
SICK은 이 세 가지 가운데 어느 것이 가장 좋은 방법이라고 말하지는 않고 있습니다. 대신 중요한 것은 자신의 상황과 목표에 맞는 선택을 하는 것이라고 강조합니다. 또한 이직을 꼭 처음부터 다시 시작하는 것으로 생각할 필요도 없다고 조언합니다. 지금까지 쌓아온 경험과 기술은 생각보다 훨씬 다양한 분야에서 활용될 수 있기 때문입니다.
결국 성공적인 이직은 단순히 회사를 옮기는 것이 아니라 자신의 강점과 가치관을 이해하고 또 그것을 가장 잘 살릴 수 있는 새로운 환경을 찾는 과정입니다. 지금 새로운 출발을 고민하고 있다면 먼저 어디로 갈까 보다 나는 어떤 사람인가를 스스로 물어보는 것이 성공적인 커리어 전환의 첫걸음이 될 수 있습니다.
더 많은 이야기가 궁금하신가요? 애플 포드캐스트, 구글 포드캐스트, 스포티파이 또는 여러분의 포드캐스트를 통해 만나보세요.

# Write unit tests with Jest

This skill describes how to design, write, run, and maintain unit tests using Jest. It covers how to analyze code under test, structure test files, choose matchers and test patterns, mock dependencies, handle async and time-based code, integrate with TypeScript and React, run tests and coverage, and avoid common pitfalls. window: that can be kind of put into this frame. A very simple example is probably where you see the word capacity the most at a restaurant. If a given restaurant has the capacity to, let's say, seat 150 people, but their processes, the way that they route their servers, for example, don't allow for that number of people to be served,

we have a mismatch in the capacity and the ability. On the other hand, you can also have the opposite problem, where you have a highly efficient waitstaff and simply not enough room to maximize that ability. In this case, your ability outpaces your capacity.

Keen listeners will recognize that this episode is coming out on a Tuesday, whereas usually episodes of the show come out on Mondays and Wednesdays and Fridays. And in fact, we've missed our Friday refills for two weeks in a row. This is a capacity problem.

Certainly with over 900 episodes of the show published, I have very likely have the ability to execute on these episodes. But because my time has been constrained, for example, yesterday, my son ended up having a fever. And so I had to spend my time doing family things rather than recording for the podcast. My capacity was limited. So why is this important?

As you go through your career, you're going to have numerous occasions where these two things will be aligned. But then you're going to have a lot of occasions where they're not aligned. And here's the critical thing. You may not actually know. You may not know that your capacity is the limiting factor or that your ability is the limiting factor.

By having this lens available, you can ask the question, is my capacity the limiting factor in this scenario? You can ask this for teams as well. The most simple example, of course, is having a highly efficient team but not having enough people on the team.

It's important to understand also that as you change one factor, another factor may change. And that your capacity is not something that you can't change. We aren't talking about external factors that are out of your control. Instead, we're talking about longer-term setup factors.

Another simple example of this is that perhaps you have the capacity to work in a particular language. You've proven this by working in that language in the past. But since it's been a while since you worked in that language, it's possible that if it came down to it in the moment, you wouldn't have the ability. And some of this is just because

Our abilities change over time. We lose abilities. They may decay with a lack of use. And the same is true if you were to imagine that you have the capacity to work in a language that you've never worked in before. In other words, if you were to learn that language, you could develop the ability to work in that language.

Another way to think about capacity is to imagine that it's similar to potential. And on the flip side, you can imagine that ability is similar to performance. You have performance and you have potential. And it should be noted that these things can change even on a day-to-day basis. As we already mentioned with the delays on recording this episode of the podcast...

window: For example, hiring an expert. If you hire an expert, you may get a lot of benefit out of that expert's knowledge. But if you allow that expert to work alone, it's very possible that they will end up creating a silo.

Because of their expertise, it's possible that if you allow them to kind of do their thing, right, then they end up doing things, creating things that may be really difficult for other developers to understand. And that creates a bottleneck. That creates a situation where a developer is siloed. And so if that developer chooses to leave...

then no one has context. No one knows how to manage what they left behind. This can make software unreliable. It can make other developers feel afraid to touch the code. Now, often we wouldn't think that hiring an expert could have a negative impact on our team, and that's because decisions are complex.
systems affect everything in the system. There's very few decisions that won't affect something else, both adversely and positively. This is true for even the smallest of actions.

Even the smallest thing like an emoji. This seems crazy, but the emojis that you send to people's Slack messages, or if you send GIFs back in text message threads, these are reinforcement mechanisms. These are ways of expressing yourself, and the other person will receive these expressions as feedback on their actions.
You can either positively reinforce actions that have positive effects on your team, or you can positively reinforce actions that have negative effects on your team.

And then you can also use the other side, negative reinforcement on things that may have negative impact on your team. And as it turns out, even though it's not intuitive, we often provide negative reinforcement for behaviors that could have positive impacts on our team. This is the example that we talked about earlier where we encourage someone to withdraw, to not bring their ideas to the table by shooting them down too harshly.
So it's important to kind of create some heuristics for yourself. For example, it's very likely that a good heuristic is to avoid negative feedback unless something is relatively critical.

Negative feedback is a very strong mechanism that we can use in the workplace. The reason for that is because given enough negative feedback, a person may fear that their job is in danger. This is especially true for managers.

And so negative feedback ends up speaking much louder than positive feedback. Positive feedback may give me the hope of some kind of better position, maybe a raise. But the downside of getting fired is much larger than the upside of getting a raise.

So, part of the practice of doing deep learning is the process of running the training process and then looking at the results. Yeah. And specifically, there's all kinds of neat things you can do with that holdout set. And so one of the things that we spent a lot of time on with the FastAI library is to try to make it easy to use best practices for debugging and testing your model. And so, for example, one of the things we find really useful is to pick the top 10 most badly predicted items in your validation set.

So for example, if there was an item where the model said, I am 99.9% sure this is a dog, and actually it's a cat, then you want to know about that situation, like which of the images that it was really confident and really wrong about. So we have a method that will actually display a grid showing you those images on your computer, show you what they should have been labeled, and show you what the model labeled them.

And so you can see what's going on. And so often what you'll find is that actually your label was wrong. You'll look at it and you'll say, oh, the computer was right and the data was wrong. And so one of the things we have in FastDI is a little GUI where you can actually, it'll pop up the ones that have been badly misclassified. And if it's actually been labeled wrongly, you can change the label.

Or maybe it wasn't a dog or a cat at all. It was actually, you know, it was the word dog or the word cat or a book about dogs or cats without a picture. And so with the FastAI library in this GUI, you can just select some things to delete because they shouldn't be part of this problem at all. You can do things like find which pairs of classes you mix up the most often.

Los Algodones has built itself up to serve the dental needs of Americans and Canadians. And the town has become wildly successful in this goal. Then a series of policy changes depleted the soil and dammed the flow of the Colorado River into Mexico. By the '60s, riverbeds were drying up. And crops were struggling. Not guilty by reason of insanity under California's McNaughton standard. This is the one everyone thinks about when they hear insanity plea. And it's also the hardest to pull off, Bob. Here's what McNaughton requires. You have to prove the burden is on the defense here, not the prosecution. That the moment you committed the act, you either didn't understand the nature of what you were doing,
or you didn't understand that it was morally wrong, it's a high bar.

It's not, I was having a mental health crisis. That's not, my medication was off. That's complete detachment from reality. Believing your parents are demons, thinking God commanded you to do it. Not understanding what a knife does to the human body. That sort of thinking. And here's the problem for Nick Reiner. Hours before his parents were found dead, he was at Conan O'Brien's Christmas party. Multiple sources reported

that he argued with his father there, got into it with Bill Hader. Witnesses described him as disruptive, acting strangely, interrupting conversations. But he was arguing. He was engaging. He was present enough to disagree with people about things. Legal experts have already waited on this. Former prosecutor Nima Rahmani, who's been on the show many a times, put it bluntly, if you're capable enough to have an argument with your parents at a Christmas party, you're not legally insane.
The standard requires total psychosis, thinking your victims are aliens, complete inability to distinguish right from wrong. Having a bad night at a party doesn't meet that standard.

Professor Lori Levinson at Loya Law School said the insanity defense is actually really tough to win. It depends entirely on what experts say about whether the defendant had a mental disease or defect severe enough that he didn't know what he was doing or didn't know it was wrong. That's the bar, basically. Nationally, only one...
about 1% of criminal defendants even attempt an insanity defense, and of those, most fail. So if full insanity is there, it's a long shot.

What's behind door number two, Bob? Well, this is where it gets even more interesting and honestly more likely. California abolished something called diminished capacity back in 82. After the Dan White case, you might know it as the Twinkie defense, even though that's not actually what happened. But that's the story for another day. The point is California voters were so outraged by the verdict that they eliminated diminished capacity as a full defense.

Here's what survived. Here's what could be behind door number two. Mental illness can still be used to challenge the specific intent required for first degree murder. First degree murder in California requires premeditation, deliberation. The prosecution has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant planned the killing.

through and through, acted with specific intent. If the defense can show that Nick Reiner's mental state at the time, his schizoaffective disorder, the medication change reportedly made a month before the killings, whatever was happening in his brain that night prevented him from forming that specific intent, the charges could be reduced. Not dismissed, but reduced. First degree murder becomes second degree murder or voluntary manslaughter. The death penalty comes off the table. Life without parole becomes life with the possibility of parole or something less.

This skill produces systematic, verifiable cash flow projections for one or more rental properties over a chosen forecast horizon. window: So the first tip is don't be a closet learner. Don't be a closet learner. This one may seem kind of strange to some of you, but learning in the dark is going to be incredibly difficult. You need everyone around you to know that you are a learner. You need your boss, your colleagues, and if you are a manager, those you manage, they all need to know that you are a learner, that you are dedicated to learning. Now, why is this so important?

Well, for quite a few reasons. First, they know you're a learner, so they will naturally come to you when they learn something new, because that's common ground. When they learn something new, then they're going to talk to somebody who cares about learning.

And perhaps you will learn something in that process as well. Second, if your boss encounters a project that he knows requires learning, he may have more of a tendency to look to you to acquire those skills because he knows that you're interested in learning.

This is a huge opportunity because it's almost like inception. Most bosses don't really want to give a free pass to employees to spend a ton of time learning techniques unless they know for certain that the efforts are well-founded and that the learning is necessary from a cash flow perspective. So by your boss being the one to bring you the project rather than the other way around,

You can explore the learning space with less hindances because you know that the cash flow problems are taken care of. You know that there is an adequate demand for this particular learning scenario. Next, other developers will likely admire your tenacity to learn, and you'll become well-respected in your job as an authority over new technology.

So there's quite a few reasons why you may want to not be a closet learner, why instead you'll want to tell other people about what you're doing. But you don't want to get too specific about what kind of learning you are doing because it may suggest that you are jumping too quickly between technologies. The reality is when you're in learning mode, you may jump from one technology to another without taking a ton of time to focus on any single thing.

Of course, you should be focusing quite a bit of time on some things whenever you find something that is worthwhile to focus a significant amount of time on. But it's a good idea to not tell everyone every single detail about what you are learning, but rather let them know about your principled stand that learning is incredibly important.

And you don't really want to tell everyone exactly when you are learning something new or what you are learning because that actually leads to our next tip. The second tip is once you have identified a positive opportunity for learning, don't expose that to your coworkers yet.

Now, you want to talk to them at some point. Obviously, sharing information, sharing the learning process is incredibly important. But learning requires failure. And even though that failure is necessary, seeing someone else fail might incite doubt into the person who is seeing that failure.

So you want to be very careful when sharing your learning experiences as doing so too early when you're still in constant failure stage may lead people to doubt that your focus on learning is actually paying off.

A new report warns the quantum threat to crypto is now practical, with public key exposure on blockchains creating a harvest now, crack later risk as powerful quantum computers come into reach. Authored by Qantas, a layer 1 focused on protecting crypto from quantum threats, the study ties advances in quantum hardware to an increasingly imminent risk.

Industry discussions center on migration strategies for quantum-resistant signatures, favoring gradual hybrid transitions over abrupt changes while addressing governance and scaling. Bitcoin is trading near $73,500 in the period covered by the report. An estimated 2.3 million to 3.7 million Bitcoin wallets could be inaccessible and non-migratable to quantum-resistant addresses, risking permanent loss when attacks become feasible.

Hardware limits challenge wallets, as larger post-quantum schemes demand more memory and compute power, affecting wallet design and user experience. Preparation varies. NIST has standardized post-quantum encryption, and firms like Google, Cynal, Apple, and Cloudflare are deploying protections with migration targets around 2029 to 2030.

Some propose hard deadline migrations to quantum-safe accounts to avoid lingering vulnerabilities, warning that tokens in unmigrated accounts could be permanently frozen. A suggested remedy is a firm deadline for token migration to quantum-safe accounts, after which unmigrated tokens would be frozen to mitigate risk. The report notes cryptocurrencies cannot update encryption via patches and public keys remain permanently exposed on blockchains, increasing long-term vulnerability.

Experts caution that rushing migration could induce bugs, so a gradual, hybrid transition is favored to balance risk mitigation with preparedness for a quantum era. Recent breakthroughs by Google, IBM, and Quantinuum suggest lower quantum resources are needed to break elliptic curve cryptography, accelerating the timeline for potential attacks.

A state chartered bank is moving to a national footprint, a shift that could position it at the center of crypto banking nationwide. United Texas Bank cleared a key hurdle when the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency approved its conversion to a national bank on May 15, 2026, opening access to federal payment rails and full trust powers.

CEO Scott Beck frames UTB as a bridge between crypto firms and traditional finance as Wall Street increasingly eyes digital assets. UTB has operated under a Federal Reserve consent order linked to Bank Secrecy Act compliance, and the OCC plan notes actions to address related enforcement matters.

As a nationally chartered bank, UTB plans to launch UTB Atomic, a 24-7 real-time liquidity payment network backed by UTB Prism Sentinel, an AI-driven real-time blockchain surveillance and compliance system. The rollout of UTB Atomic and Prism Sentinel is part of a broader digital asset custody and trust services plan slated for summer 2026.
